title: The weaver
hookLine: a weaver lies down on the river steps in the dark, waiting for a teacher's foot
tomorrow: if not in a temple or a mosque, where does Kabir say God is?

lines: A GIFT ON A LAP LOOM.
A WEAVER ON THE RIVER STEPS.
cards: Some gifts take a week of evenings. Zoe is making one on a little lap loom, for Theo's sister Hannah, who's getting married soon.
Far from Zoe's couch, and long ago, in the city of Kashi on the Ganges, a young weaver lies down across the stone steps by the river. It's still dark.
He's heard that a well-known teacher, Ramananda, comes down these steps before dawn to bathe, and the teacher hasn't taken him as a student. So he waits in the path. Footsteps.
A foot lands on him. The startled teacher cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram.

teach.h: RAM: A NAME FROM A TEACHER'S MOUTH.
teach.b: The weaver is Kabir, and in the story he stands up with what he came for: God's name, from a teacher's mouth. That's how a student is started on the path, and Kabir took that cry as his start.
It's a legend, told more than one way. But look at who's in it.

teach.h: MUSLIM WEAVERS, HINDU TEACHER, SIKH BOOK.
teach.b: Kabir grew up in a family of Muslim weavers; in a hymn kept in the Sikh scripture, he calls himself a weaver of Kashi. He learned the name from a Hindu teacher.
And his songs sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs bow to. Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all claim him, and he belongs to none of them alone. Now the teaching.
The Ram that Kabir sings isn't the prince of the epics with a bow. It's God without form, beyond every picture, and Kabir loves that God anyway, with his whole heart.

teach.h: NIRGUN BHAKTI: LOVE WITHOUT AN IMAGE.
teach.b: Teachers call it nirgun bhakti: devotion to God without qualities, no image, no one building. And he sang it at the loom.

teach.h: THE SHAWL, GIVEN BACK AS IT WAS.
teach.b: A song sung in Kabir's name pictures the body as a fine shawl, woven by God thread by thread.
Gods, sages and ordinary people wore it and stained it. Kabir, the song says, wore it with care and laid it down just as it was given. So the weaving wasn't a break from the prayer.
The shuttle going back and forth was where he sang it, and he signed the songs: says Kabir.

how: Kabir's songs are sung as bhajans by Hindu devotees, in Sikh kirtan from the Guru Granth Sahib, and in the Kabir Panth, a community that follows his teaching.

o: a scribe who stitched old scriptures into a book
a craftsman who wove cloth for temple images
Kabir, the poet who sang God's name at his loom

games.q: who's in the weaver's story? tap the pairs.
p: the teacher on the steps before dawn
the name cried out in the dark
love for God without form or image
the body, woven by God, given back

s: Kabir belongs to just one of the religions that claim him
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all claim him; he belongs to none of them alone.
the Ram in Kabir's songs is the prince of the epics with his bow
Kabir's Ram is God without form, beyond every picture: nirgun bhakti.
a song in Kabir's name pictures the body as a shawl woven by God
others stained it; Kabir, the song says, laid it down just as it was given.

games.q: you're Kabir. the teacher you want hasn't taken you as a student. what do you do?
o: lie down on the river steps in the dark, in his path
find a different teacher who'll say yes right away
give up on teachers and go back to the loom
games.why: in the legend he lies across the steps; Ramananda steps on him, cries 'Ram, Ram', and Kabir takes the name as his start.

practice: Find a piece of string: a shoelace, a strand of yarn, a ribbon from a drawer. Tie one slow knot, untie it, and tie it again, at the pace of your breathing.
In Kabir's song the cloth is lent, so handle the thread like something you'll hand back.

wordCard.voice: The weaver: Kabir, who sang God's name at the loom, and whose shawl, in the song, went back unstained.

orig.note: Hindi: weaver. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir calls himself a weaver of Kashi.

carryVoice: Your line: the weaver. Three houses claim him, and he belongs to none alone. Kabir, one of eight.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 482 (Raag Asa, Kabir: 'you are a Brahmin, I am a weaver of Kashi')
the legend of Kabir and Ramananda on the ghat steps (hagiographic tradition after Nabhadas's Bhaktamal)
'Jhini jhini bini chadariya' (the finely woven shawl), a song sung in Kabir's name
